newsitem.title: GERMANY: German watchdog probes Daimler disclosure.
newsitem.headline: German watchdog probes Daimler disclosure.

text.p: German securities watchdog BAWe is looking into Daimler-Benz AG's financial disclosure policies after a Daimler board member provided reporters with approximate figures for the firm's 1996 results.

Spokesman for the Federal Securities Supervision Authority (BAWe) Juergen Oberfrank told Reuters on Wednesday that it was too early to say if the Daimler executive had broken any rules on disclosure which are meant to ensure a fair dissemination of financial results here.
At issue were remarks made by Daimler management board member Eckard Cordes to reporters attending a dinner at the Geneva car show.
Cordes said Daimler-Benz's group 1996 net profit would be more than two billion marks ($1.2 billion) and sales around 107 billion marks. Daimler reported a 5.7 billion mark loss in 1995.
A Daimler spokesman on Tuesday would not confirm the figures, telling Reuters that official results will not be made public until the company holds its annual press conference next month.
The BAWe has to establish whether the disclosure should have come via a so-called "ad-hoc" electronic transmission, which German law requires for potentially market-moving information.
Sometimes failure to report via the "ad-hoc" route can consitute a violation of Germany's insider trading rules.
German securities law allows penalties of up to five years in jail for insider trading and jail terms have been so far imposed in two of the seven cases imposed.

A piece of insider information is described in German law as "every fact that it not yet publicly known...which is capable of having a considerable effect on the price of the insider security, should it be announced publicly."
In a separate case, the BAWe was in the news last month when it announced that the Frankfurt District Court had ruled that a so-called "primary insider" should be fined for illegal insider trading.
A primary insider is usually an employee of a company concerned in an insider trade.
The watchdog declined to name the individual concerned, which said it had been ordered to pay a fine of one million marks.
